title: Turn a humanoid's hung upper body round on its gantry hook so that its back faces you
instruction: Turn the body hanging from the swivel hook half a turn, so its back faces you.
context: Robots that build robots must handle robots under assembly. Menlo Research's open-source humanoid Asimov 1 is built hanging from a gantry hook, and its build guide's step 10.6 reads: "Turn the robot around so we can now work on the back cover." On a swivel hook the body turns freely: the push that starts it loads it with momentum that the hook's drag takes well over a full turn to remove, so to leave it at rest facing away the push must be judged or the spin taken out by hand: a late catch overshoots, and a hard block is a blow to the hand and the robot. Here the upper body (torso shell, both arms and the head, 18.3 kg, yaw inertia 0.26 kg m2) hangs alone on a bench gantry: a stand-in for the whole hung robot, whose legs would not clear the table within the arms' reach.
setup: Two YAM arms at the near edge of a table; positions are (x forward from the arm bases, y left) in cm, heights above the table. A bench gantry of 40 mm square steel stands over the table: posts at y = 40 and -40 and a beam between them, 83 cm up. Its ball-bearing swivel hook, at (55, 0), carries Asimov 1's upper body by its shoulder shackles: the torso shell, both arms hanging straight and the head, 18.3 kg, 71 cm from head to hands, 42 cm across the arms and 22 cm front to back. Its centre of mass is 35 cm above the table and its hands about 3 cm above it. It turns about the hook's vertical axis; its yaw inertia there is 0.26 kg m2, and a free spin from 45 deg/s slows to 27.5 deg/s in 10 s and still turns at 8 deg/s after 35 s. At the start it hangs still, facing the arms. The mark: turned 180 degrees, its back square to the arms. The arms start at their ready pose.
scoring: Real trial: a camera above tracks marks on the body's shoulders (yaw at 20 Hz or faster, the net angle counted through full turns, the rate from one frame to the next); a side video shows the hands. On the mark: turned 180 degrees net, within 10 degrees, either way round; past that, or a full turn more, is not on the mark. 0 at any time: a blow (the spin slows or reverses by more than 25 deg/s within 0.1 s, about 11 N at 10 cm from the swivel); a collision (it changes by more than 5 deg/s within 0.1 s while turning faster than 10 deg/s, with no fingertip within 5 cm of the body); left spinning (over 20 deg/s at the end). 1.0: still (under 1 deg/s) on the mark and staying there, for 1 s, however it got there: the net angle, and where the hook's drag would carry it (the angle plus 20 s times the rate, the swivel's measured spin-down), both on the mark; the trial then ends. 0.25: otherwise, turned through 90 degrees or more and stopped (under 5 deg/s) at some time. Anything else scores 0.
fidelity: Rigid bodies at 240 Hz on GPU. The upper body is one rigid body: the maker's URDF links merged at the zero pose, the arms rigid and hanging straight (lock them in a real trial), each link's convex hull its collider. It yaws on a revolute joint at the hook with PhysX joint friction 0.005; the shackles and chains are not modelled, so it does not swing or tilt. Distances to the body are measured to those hulls.
